research_context.root_cause_received: The application's database connection pool is exhausted due to slow and timing-out database queries, leading to the application becoming unresponsive and failing to serve requests.

solutions.title: Increase database connection pool size
solutions.description: Raise the max_connections in PostgreSQL and the pool_size in your application's DB config (e.g., SQLAlchemy pool_size, Django CONN_MAX_AGE). This directly addresses pool exhaustion shown in app-error.log.
pros: Immediately addresses the root cause (pool exhaustion)
Low-risk config change if DB server has headroom
cons: Each DB connection consumes ~5-10MB RAM on the server
Root cause of *why* pool grew may still exist (slow queries, leak)

solutions.title: Add a connection pooler (PgBouncer)
solutions.description: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction-mode pooling between your app and PostgreSQL. It multiplexes many app connections onto fewer real DB connections.
pros: Handles connection storms without changing DB max_connections
Industry-standard solution for high-connection PostgreSQL workloads
cons: Requires deployment of a new component (ops overhead)
Transaction-mode breaks session-level features (SET, advisory locks)
Not instant — needs testing before production rollout

solutions.title: Kill long-running/idle DB connections immediately
solutions.description: Run: SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'idle' AND query_start < NOW() - INTERVAL '5 minutes'; This frees leaked connections right now without a restart.
pros: Safe to run on production without downtime
cons: Symptom fix only — does not prevent recurrence
May abort in-progress transactions (check state carefully)

solutions.title: Restart the application service
solutions.description: sudo systemctl restart your-app. Forces all app-side connections to close and the pool to reset.
cons: Causes brief outage (30s–2min depending on startup time)
Does not fix the root cause
Should not be attempted before trying sol_3
